clue.text: Right wing pals assembled outside university, April 30th

indicators.note: Anything assembled has been put together afresh, so the letters named are free to stand in any order.
What is outside something encloses it, so the shuffled letters close round the university's single letter and take it into the mix.

parts.note: anagram fodder, 13 letters
u = university, the letter the shuffled pals surround

explanation.surface: Friends on the political right gathering outside a university on the last day of April.
explanation.walkthrough: The night of 30 April is kept across Germany and Scandinavia with bonfires, the eve on which witches were said to gather. 'Right wing pals' looks like a definition and is thirteen letters of fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Walpurgis Night is the night of 30 April, the eve of St Walpurga's feast, so the date names the occasion itself.

clue.text: Star group's uncovered landau touring airfield

indicators.note: Take the cover off a word and the letters at each end come away, leaving the middle exposed.
A tour goes right round its destination, so the letters doing the touring wrap around the next chunk.

parts.note: LANDAU uncovered loses its outer L and U
'drome is the clipped everyday form of aerodrome, an airfield

explanation.surface: An open carriage being driven round an airfield.
explanation.walkthrough: A landau is a horse-drawn carriage with a folding hood, so 'uncovered landau' first reads as the hood down rather than as two letters gone. Airfields shed their first syllable in speech long ago.
explanation.definitionFit: Andromeda is the constellation named for the chained princess of Greek myth, a group of stars lying between Pegasus and Perseus.

clue.text: Chubby lads in Lilliput, titchy

indicators.note: What is in something sits inside it, and here the letters sit unbroken inside the words that follow.

parts.note: hidden in LilliPUT, TItchy, running straight over the comma

explanation.surface: Small plump boys in the land of tiny people.
explanation.walkthrough: Lilliput is the island of six-inch people in Gulliver's Travels, so 'titchy' reads as a remark about it rather than as more letters to hide among. Punctuation never interrupts a hidden word.
explanation.definitionFit: Putti are the chubby winged infants carved and painted all over Renaissance art, the plural of putto.

clue.text: Managed my no-frills accommodation, full of bitterness

parts.note: to run a business is to manage it, so managed is ran
cor is a British exclamation of surprise, like 'my!'

indicators.note: the frills are the edges, so cutting them leaves only the inside of the word

parts.note: a house is accommodation

explanation.surface: Someone who ran a budget guesthouse ended up deeply resentful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no-frills' trims HOUSE to its middle, OUS. 'My' here is the exclamation, not the possessive: cor is British slang for the same surprise.
explanation.definitionFit: Rancorous means marked by rancour, a deep and long-lasting resentment or bitterness.

clue.text: Norwegian playmaker starts for Ipswich, bags three points

indicators.note: starts means the first letters of the following words

parts.note: the first letter of each word is wanted
S, E and N are three points of the compass: south, east and north

explanation.surface: A Norwegian midfielder makes his first appearances for Ipswich Town and scores enough to win the match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Playmaker' suggests a football midfielder, a sense backed by Ipswich (an English football club) and three points for a win, but it means a maker of plays.
explanation.definitionFit: Henrik Ibsen was the Norwegian dramatist of A Doll's House, so a maker of plays.

clue.text: Final appearance of Ian Lavender working US ranch

indicators.note: Something working is in motion, and letters in motion will not stay in the order they were given.
Where a name makes its final appearance is its last letter, and that letter alone is wanted.

parts.note: the final letter of Ian
anagram fodder, 8 letters

explanation.surface: The last screen role of Ian Lavender, filmed on a ranch in America.
explanation.walkthrough: Ian Lavender played Private Pike in Dad's Army, so 'final appearance' reads as a line from an obituary rather than an instruction to take one letter. Michael Jackson named his California estate after the island in Peter Pan.
explanation.definitionFit: Neverland was Michael Jackson's California ranch, complete with funfair and zoo, named after the island children fly to in Peter Pan.

clue.text: Brave knight left adult daughter a pretty cockatoo

indicators.note: Whoever has left is gone, so the letters named depart from the name that held them.

parts.note: Sir Galahad, the purest knight of the Round Table
a = adult, the old film certificate; it goes
d = daughter in family trees and directory entries; it goes too

explanation.surface: A gallant knight leaving a handsome bird to his grown-up daughter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' is a will-reading verb in the surface and a departure in the wordplay, and the two letters that walk off are the end of the knight's name. The bird itself is the pink-and-grey cockatoo of inland Australia, whose name doubles as Australian slang for a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: The galah is the rose-pink and grey cockatoo that flocks across inland Australia, a handsome bird by any measure.

clue.text: Climbing frame exhausted Trevor Peters (the novelist)

indicators.note: Something exhausted has had everything drained out of it, so the word keeps only its first and last letters.

parts.note: Trevor drained of its insides keeps T and R
Ellis Peters was the pen name Edith Pargeter wrote the Brother Cadfael mysteries under

explanation.surface: A climbing frame that wore out a novelist called Trevor Peters.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracket is doing real work: it says which Peters is meant, the one whose first name was borrowed for the Cadfael mysteries. 'Climbing frame' is playground equipment until the plants get hold of it.
explanation.definitionFit: A trellis is the lattice fixed to a wall for climbing plants to scramble up — a frame for climbing, not for climbing on.

clue.text: Reprimand moggy, having crapped inside on a regular basis

indicators.note: What goes inside sits within, so the letters just found drop into the middle of the word already named.

parts.note: moggy is British affection for an ordinary, non-pedigree cat

indicators.note: Doing something on a regular basis means at even intervals, so every second letter is picked out.

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters of cRaPpEd

explanation.surface: Telling off a cat that keeps soiling the house indoors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On a regular basis' looks like a description of the cat's habits and is an instruction to count letters in twos. The reprimand sense comes from a summons onto the rug in front of the boss's desk.
explanation.definitionFit: To carpet someone is to give them a dressing-down, from the old summons onto the carpet to be told off.

clue.text: Check gold and diamonds investment after being cleaned out

parts.note: Au is the chemical symbol for gold, from Latin aurum
D is how the suit is written on a bridge scorecard

indicators.note: A word cleaned out has had its contents taken, leaving only the letters standing at each end.

parts.note: INVESTMENT cleaned out keeps only its I and T

explanation.surface: Checking a gold and diamond investment after thieves have emptied the safe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Check' sits at the front looking like part of the shopping list rather than the definition. Gold and diamonds are both worth banking as shorthand — one a chemical symbol, the other a card suit.
explanation.definitionFit: An audit is a formal check of the books, the noun a company's accounts are put through once a year.

clue.text: City finish off Aston Villa — he's getting sacked

indicators.note: Getting sacked is being thrown out, and letters thrown out land in a new order.
To finish off a word is to take the letter it finishes on and nothing else.

parts.note: the last letter of Aston
anagram fodder, 8 letters

explanation.surface: City beat Aston Villa and the Villa manager loses his job for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'City' in a football surface is half a club's name, and here it is only a place on a map. Aston Villa are the Birmingham club, which is what makes the sacking sound like a manager's.
explanation.definitionFit: Nashville is the capital of Tennessee and the home of country music, so 'City' is the plain category it belongs to.

clue.text: President features in video plug next month

indicators.note: To feature in something is to appear inside it, so the piece named goes within the one that follows.

parts.note: a promo is the short film made to plug something
Xi Jinping, president of China

explanation.surface: A head of state turning up in a promotional video due out next month.
explanation.walkthrough: Proximo is the counting-house Latin for next month, twin of 'ultimo' for last month, still met in old business letters. A president of two letters is one every solver should now expect.
explanation.definitionFit: Proximo means 'of next month' in commercial usage, as in an invoice falling due on the 15th proximo.

clue.text: Ran around with young Prince Harry, the horny beast!

indicators.note: Something sent around is turned about, so the letters named are read back the other way.

parts.note: RAN turned about
w is the standard short form of with, as on a prescription
Hal is the old pet form of Harry, and Shakespeare's young Prince Hal is Henry V before the crown

explanation.surface: Racing about with the young prince, who is a randy so-and-so.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Horny beast' is an insult in the surface and a flat description in the answer: one tooth, grown out through the lip into a spiral tusk. The prince is Shakespeare's Harry, not the modern one.
explanation.definitionFit: The narwhal is the Arctic whale whose left tooth grows into a long spiral tusk, making it literally a beast with a horn.

clue.text: Costner led its cast — lowest cast, by the sound of it

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the 1987 gangster film starring Kevin Costner as Eliot Ness

definitions.text: lowest cast, by the sound of it
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the lowest caste in the Indian caste system, caste sounding just like cast

explanation.surface: Kevin Costner heads a film cast that sounds like the lowest of the low.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By the sound of it' asks you to hear cast as caste: the Untouchables, now called Dalits, were the group outside and below India's four castes.
explanation.definitionFit: The title names both the film and the outcast group, so one phrase meets both readings.

clue.text: Rendered invalid, I'd suffered with Nile flu

indicators.note: Someone who has suffered has been knocked about, and letters knocked about come out in a different order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, 2 letters
anagram fodder, 7 letters

explanation.surface: Someone laid low by a bug picked up on the Nile.
explanation.walkthrough: West Nile fever is a real mosquito-borne illness, which is what makes 'Nile flu' sound like a diagnosis rather than seven letters to shuffle. 'Rendered invalid' keeps the sick man in plain sight, stressed the other way.
explanation.definitionFit: To nullify something is to render it invalid — to cancel it so that it carries no force.

clue.text: Measure fit for wooden shoes?

definitions.meaning: the surface takes it as sizing a foot; the sense wanted is the old one, something you tread to music
not shoes that fit, but steps suited to hard wooden soles, which hammer the rhythm out on the boards

explanation.surface: Taking a measurement so that a pair of wooden shoes will fit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Measure' is the hinge: the sense that survives in 'tread a measure', not the one that comes with a tape. Lancashire mill workers wore wooden-soled shoes and beat the time out with them on stone floors.
explanation.definitionFit: A clog dance is a step performed in wooden-soled shoes, and a measure is an old word for a dance, so the clue describes it straight through.

clue.text: Nelly getting excited when cuddling fit Welsh lad

definitions.note: Llewellyn is a Welsh man's name, not a word meaning a Welshman, so 'Welsh lad' defines by example.

indicators.note: Someone getting excited will not keep still, and letters that will not keep still change places.
To cuddle something is to get your arms right round it, so the letters open and take the next word inside.

parts.note: NELLY with its letters rearranged
someone fit is well, in good health

explanation.surface: An excited Nelly throwing her arms round a good-looking boy from Wales.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fit' in the surface is the modern compliment about someone's looks; the wordplay wants the older sense, in good health. The name itself belonged to the medieval princes of Gwynedd.
explanation.definitionFit: Llewellyn is a Welsh man's name, borne by the princes of Gwynedd who fought the English kings, so a lad from Wales may well be one.

clue.text: US chemist's rosier update on "Elizabeth: annus horribilis"?

definitions.meaning: the straight half, hiding in a possessive: the American who worked out how to make rubber hold its shape
the Queen's name for her terrible 1992; put her successor on the throne, make the year a happy one, and you have said the name

explanation.surface: A cheerier sequel to the Queen's description of her worst year on the throne.
explanation.walkthrough: The Queen used the Latin in a 1992 speech, after the Windsor Castle fire and the collapse of three of her children's marriages. Swap the monarch, cheer the year up, and the chemist is named.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Goodyear was the American chemist who discovered vulcanisation, and his name read as two words is the opposite of a horrible year for the present king.

clue.text: Part of Tuchel's earlier team

indicators.note: Only a part of what follows is wanted, and that part runs letter for letter through the words as they stand.

parts.note: hidden in TuCHEL'S EArlier

explanation.surface: Some of the squad Thomas Tuchel used to manage.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Tuchel managed in west London, and won the Champions League there, before Bayern and the England job. The letters run straight through the apostrophe — punctuation never counts in a hidden word.
explanation.definitionFit: Chelsea are the west London football club Tuchel managed before Bayern and England, so 'team' is the plain category.

clue.text: Begrudge papa leaving here

indicators.note: Whoever is leaving goes out, so that letter is taken away from the word that held it.

parts.note: here = present, the word called back at a register
papa is P in the radio alphabet; it goes

explanation.surface: Grudging the fact that dad is going away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Here' answers a register: present, the word you call back when your name is read out. Papa is P in the radio alphabet, the same list that supplies alpha, bravo and charlie.
explanation.definitionFit: To resent something is to begrudge it, to go on holding it against whoever did it.

clue.text: Difficult to catch scoop paid out ten cents

indicators.note: Money paid out is money gone, so whatever it names is handed over and lost.

parts.note: a newspaper's scoop is its exclusive
X is ten in Roman numerals; it goes
c is the abbreviation for cent; it goes too

explanation.surface: A hard-to-pin-down story the paper got for all of ten cents.
explanation.walkthrough: Scoop and exclusive are the same thing in a newsroom, and that swap has to come before any letters move. Ten cents is no sum of money here: it is a Roman numeral and an abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Something elusive keeps slipping away from whoever is chasing it, which is precisely being difficult to catch.

clue.text: Like a rough diamond when sober?

definitions.meaning: a stone straight out of the ground has not yet been cut into facets
half cut is British slang for drunk, so a man not cut at all has had nothing

explanation.surface: A likeable but unpolished man, described as he is when he has not been drinking.
explanation.walkthrough: A rough diamond is a person too: warm-hearted, no manners at all. The drinking half leans on 'half cut', which is how the British say tipsy, so the opposite state takes the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: A diamond still rough from the mine has not been cut into facets, and since 'half cut' means drunk, a sober man is not cut at all.

clue.text: European turning over a fortune in bar that's legally approved

definitions.note: Only 'bar' is the synonym; 'that's legally approved' marks it as the lawyers' word for it rather than the everyday one.

indicators.note: Turning something over stands it on its head, and in a down clue that means its letters are read upwards.

parts.note: E is the standard short form of European
POTS of money is a fortune, turned over

explanation.surface: A European gambling away a fortune in a bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' is the pub in the surface and a verb in the answer, and the legal tag is the setter's promise that the word belongs to lawyers. The fortune is the one in 'pots of money'.
explanation.definitionFit: To estop someone is to bar them in law from asserting something at odds with what they previously allowed, so the legal tag says which sense of bar is wanted.

clue.text: 500 uncultured Aussie blokes who emptied a few schooners?

definitions.note: The definition arrives as a relative clause rather than a noun, and the question mark is the setter admitting it: men who empty schooners.

parts.note: D is 500 in Roman numerals
an ocker is Australian slang for a loud, unrefined man

explanation.surface: Five hundred rough Australian men who have put away a few beers.
explanation.walkthrough: A schooner is a big glass of beer in an Australian bar and a sailing ship at the quayside, and only one of the two gets emptied for a living. The question mark marks the stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: Dockers empty ships for a living, and a schooner is a ship as well as the glass of beer the surface has in mind.

clue.text: Boorish Conservative, right idiot

parts.note: C is the party's initial on a ballot paper
r is the standard short form of right
an ass is a fool

explanation.surface: A rude verdict on a Tory: the man is a complete idiot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Right' sits between a Conservative and an idiot, so it reads as the intensifier in 'a right idiot' — British for a thorough one — when the wordplay only wants its initial.
explanation.definitionFit: Crass behaviour is coarse and unfeeling, which is what calling someone boorish says about them.

clue.text: The Devil claims Sir Charlie, retired church worker

indicators.note: To claim something is to take it to yourself, so the name opens up and takes the next letters in.
Someone retired has gone back, and letters that go back are read the other way.

parts.note: the Devil's own name, which forms the shell
SIR plus C, the radio alphabet's Charlie, turned back

explanation.surface: The Devil laying claim to a retired churchman called Sir Charlie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retired' reads as an elderly clergyman and works as a reversal. The church worker wanted is the man who keeps the sacristy, looking after the vestments and sacred vessels.
explanation.definitionFit: A sacristan is the officer in charge of a church's sacristy — its vestments, vessels and plate — so church worker is his job description.

clue.text: Dropping to the floor naked, absolutely knackered

indicators.note: naked means stripped of its covering, so the outside letters are removed

parts.note: falling means dropping to the floor

explanation.surface: Someone collapses on the floor without clothes, utterly exhausted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'naked' strips F and G from FALLING. Knackered is British slang for exhausted.
explanation.definitionFit: All in is an informal British phrase for completely worn out, tired to the point of collapse.

clue.text: Doctor patented an SSRI drug

indicators.note: To doctor something is to tamper with it, and tampered-with letters come out in another order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, 14 letters

explanation.surface: A doctor taking out a patent on a new SSRI medicine.
explanation.walkthrough: An SSRI is a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor, so the fodder names the very thing it spells and the surface tells the truth twice over. 'Doctor' has to be read as the verb, to tamper with.
explanation.definitionFit: An antidepressant is the class of medicine an SSRI belongs to, so 'drug' is the plain category.
